This study presents a study on noncrystallographic groups, specifically those that combine symmetry types BC4 and interlacing pattern 2. A specific set of groups within this category has been identified and classified, comprising a total of 12 distinct types. Furthermore, a comprehensive method to systematically organize these groups in a hierarchical manner has been established. It has also been proven that there are unique sets of vectors that can effectively represent each group in this category.

We develop a system that uses a specific object's markerless pose to learn end-effector position calibration and object detection from simulated data. Our real-time algorithm leverages a pre-trained convolutional neural network to achieve this end-effector pose estimation without the need for complex calibration procedures. Our approach demonstrates accurate end-effector pose estimation and calibrated calculations in various real-world scenarios, showcasing its efficiency and simplicity.

A new research framework is introduced to analyze treatment interference in studies, with a focus on understanding how one treatment influences beyond the treated group. The framework posits that interference only occurs between treatment units in the K nearest neighbors of each observation in the target sample. A key estimation equation is developed to consistently estimate treatment effects under these conditions. The research demonstrates the effectiveness of this framework through simulation studies and real-world data analysis, which reveals that certain assumptions regarding interference may be precarious.

Calculations of neutrino energy production in core environments of stars have been conducted, considering various forms of Dark Matter and their interactions within specific fields and through distinct annihilation processes. These studies involve analyzing the effects of pseudoscalar-mediated interactions on neutrino emissions resulting from Dark Matter annihilation, with a focus on how PDG and DFSZ models behave under these conditions. To demonstrate our findings, we illustrate their potential relevance in observing supernovae events like Neutron Star mergers.

The ongoing UNIONS project, a major imaging survey of the local universe, aims to gather comprehensive shape and redshift data for nearly 300 million galaxies. In this context, we present a new pipeline called ShapePipe, designed to efficiently measure galaxy shapes on a massive scale. Specifically, we test ShapePipe's performance on a sample of 100,000 galaxies from the CFIS survey's g-band, utilizing a state-of-the-art cosmic-shear analysis method. Our results show that ShapePipe's quality control measures effectively filter out inaccuracies in shape data, yielding high-quality outcomes comparable to established pipelines. Moreover, we observe a notable trend in shape measurement accuracy based on object brightness, with the impact of this trend on weak-lensing outcomes being minimal. Our research also reveals a potential influence of measurement algorithm on higher-order galaxy-shape characteristics, suggesting the need for further investigation. Ultimately, we demonstrate that ShapePipe excels in precision, speed, and scalability, making it an ideal tool for extensive galaxy shape measurements, particularly for the UNIONS project.

Our research builds upon the work of Harman, Marstrand, and Prasad, extending their findings with respect to the flow's orbit closure and additive diophantine approximation. We introduce two novel generalizations: horizontal submanifolds are now permitted, and the projection map $\pi$ need not be linear. By combining these advancements, we establish two equidistribution results, which in turn yield two broadened versions of Harman's theorems. Moreover, our findings imply enhanced generalizations of Weyl's theorems on almost uniform diophantine approximation and a result by Berend and Shmerkin regarding orthogonal projections of a specific set.

We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain local vanishing properties for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities have been identified. These properties were also discovered separately by [FL2].

We've successfully observed a field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) phase transition in an isotropic Heisenberg spin model using a high-precision experiment based on a single crystal of two-dimensional mercury manganese. Our experimental results were obtained through EPR spectroscopy on a well-ordered sample and were in agreement with statistical thermodynamic predictions. Notably, we were able to match theoretical models with measured variables, such as crystallographic spacing and exchange interactions. Our research demonstrates BKT critical behavior in a system without geometric frustration and opens up possibilities for studying quantum Heisenberg antiferromagnets through quantum control techniques.

We investigate the possibility of dual axion-stereile neutrino dark matter within a two-field inflation model. In this context, one field drives the inflation, while the other is non-thermally produced through a resonance known as the swamping resonance. This resonance has the capability to generate sufficient axion density to account for the dark matter, occurring simultaneously with thermal generation of the sterile neutrone, which then generates the dark matter within a stockholder interval. We examine the impact of varying model parameters on the predicted abundance of both the axion and sterile neutrone dark matter, while also considering constraints from isotope searches and neutron structure levels. Ultimately, we demonstrate that stable dual axion-stereile neutrone dark matter can be produced within a considerable section of the Higgs inflation parameter space by considering a model where the heavier of the two particles dominates the dark matter following evaporation of the early universe by inflation.

We enhance the known upper bounds on the stabilizer rank for specific values of $k$. Specifically, for $\delta_{k+1} \subsetneq \delta_k$, the rank of $k+\delta_{k+1}$ is now known to be at most that of $k+\delta_k. We apply this improvement to the binary W-state to demonstrate that the stabilizer rank of $kL(3,2)$ is at most a certain quadratic expression in $k$.

This research investigates the acceleration of the universe by assuming the dark energy density is derived from the potential energy of a scalar field, taking into account Tsallis entropy in theories such as Dirac-Goto, DGP models, and the holographic dark energy model.  A complex form of the quintessence model is applied to derive the equation of state parameter, $\omega$, as a function of the scalar field $\phi$.  By analyzing the evolution of $\omega$, we examine the stability of various models by plotting them against each other in the $\omega-\dot{\omega}$ plane.  Furthermore, our results are validated using observational data from type Ia supernovae, a Hubble diagram up to a redshift of $z=2.3$, a statefinder diagram and a phase space diagram.  These examinations reveal that the models conform to a de-Sitter universe scenario in the late-time phase.

Between 2015 and 2016, 4 $K$2 plates were executed by the LAMOST as part of a dedicated time-domain survey project, utilizing a $5^\prime$ grid to scan $360^\circ$ of the sky across the North Galactic Pole to $\delta=-2^\circ$ with a $0.5^\circ$ field of view and $1.4$ arcmin slit width, all within the $u^\prime$ to $z^\prime$ band. A total of $11.8 \times 10^6$ sources were captured in the initial data reduction, with further analysis of the reduced data leading to a comprehensive catalog of $1.11 \times 10^6$ stars exhibiting significant variability across the four exposures. Utilizing a machine learning approach, this sample was divided into distinct categories of variable stars, with the data further analyzed to determine the characteristics of various star types, including their distribution across the sky, magnitude ranges, and the identification of notable areas of interest. Ultimately, this study marks a significant breakthrough in the LAMOST's capabilities as a major observational platform for significant astronomical discoveries.

Recent advancements in nanoscale technology have led to significant fluctuations in random circuit behavior, which can be leveraged to enhance the performance of hardware-based True Random Number Generators (TRNGs). A widely accepted approach involves utilizing SRAM initialization states as entropy sources for PRNG seeding or TRNG gating. This paper presents a novel method to exploit voltage fluctuations below the SRAM read threshold voltage, which can be achieved through current oversampling or supply voltage underscaling techniques. Through extensive simulations and experimental validation using TSMC 55nm SRAMs, it has been demonstrated that supply voltage underscaling not only improves generation rate but also maintains statistical reliability and security properties. Specifically, the proposed TRNG architecture, known as TuRaN, is capable of producing 128 bits of randomness per second while still meeting the stringent requirements of NIST SP 800-90B for security compliance.

A single-electron resistive switch based on a thin molecule functions as a single-electron transistor, featuring a massive tunnel junction that acts as the gate. This concept has been proposed for single-electron memory applications, with our research focusing on the design and simulation of molecular single-electron devices, specifically those consisting of gold electrodes and central molecules such as benzene-dithiol and pentacene-dithiol. Our simulations utilized the nonequilibrium Green's function approach, combined with a density functional theory framework with a hybrid exchange-correlation functional. The studies revealed a positive bias-induced current increase, accompanied by a notable conductance roll-off at high voltages, characteristic of single-electron tunneling behavior.

The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach to calculating complex multi-loop scalar Feynman integrals, offering a promising avenue to address the longstanding caustic problem. The success of this approach relies heavily on the all-plus helicity configuration, and in an effort to expand its applicability, we have developed a novel numerical framework to evaluate the causal representation. This framework is now being tested on two-loop helicity-amplitude calculations and we outline our initial results in this context.

This paper aims to provide a direct proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, which is equivalent to a one-dimensional non-self-adjoint Schrödinger equation. A direct eigenfunction expansion formula can be used to solve the non-Hermitian effective mass Schrödinger equation in one dimension.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho model for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the phase transition. By applying $\beta$-$\alpha$ equilibrium, a mass-radius relationship map is generated for mixed stars, and the resulting mass-radius map is compared with observational data from X-ray observations of neutron stars.

The introduction focuses on the impact of optical transparency and
delayed light phenomena in a deformed optomechanical setup with light-driven delay.
A specific view of the system is linked to a Hamiltonian setup, incorporating a linear
optical cavity, a driven cavity, a two-level atom, and a harmonic oscillator.
The system is studied under two distinct scenarios: when the deformation parameter equals one,
a standard optomechanical system is created, and when it differs from one, a non-linear interaction is established.
Two distinct situations are considered: one with a blue shift and one with a red shift in the pump laser frequency.
Within these contexts, the system exhibits both a decrease in optical pumping and a decrease in time.
The study also investigates how these phenomena are influenced by system parameters,
including the deformation parameter, intensity, and decoherence rate.

In a previous study, it was found that certain R-parity broken states, particularly those with a 3-3-1 1 configuration, could be effectively modeled using a two-multiple rigid body framework where one component represented a rotational degree of freedom and the other an irrep SU(3). Building upon this study, we now examine R-parity broken states with a 1 1 1 configuration within the same theoretical framework, and demonstrate that their characteristics can be consistently represented by a system of two interconnected rotators. Furthermore, we propose a method to approximate the wave functions of these states using products of SU(3) states, and examine how this approximation compares with the wave functions obtained from the dynamic SU(3)×U(6)⊗U(1) model, which incorporates R-parity broken 3-3-1 1 states.

The growth of ultrathin films made from transition metal compounds in a vacuum has become a key tool for studying the magnetic, electronic, and structural properties of these materials. The ability to create such films in a vacuum has enabled researchers to explore the unique behaviors of thin films that differ from their bulk counterparts, offering new insights into the fundamental physics of magnetic systems. The unique properties of ultrathin films arise from their distinct structural and electronic characteristics, which are influenced by factors such as strain and dimensionality. The lattice structure of these materials can be modified through strain, leading to changes in the orbital energy levels and spin-orbit coupling, which in turn affects the magnetic and electronic behavior of the system. The confinement of electrons within a few atomic layers also leads to the emergence of novel phenomena, such as changes in the Fermi surface topology and enhanced fluctuations in spin and orbital degrees of freedom. The ultra-high vacuum environment used to grow these films allows for the application of advanced spectroscopic techniques, providing new information about the spin and orbital dynamics of these materials and their relationship to the superconductivity observed in similar bulk materials.

We've developed a theoretical framework to study the behavior of laser-cooled atoms in a specific type of environment. This environment consists of atoms cooled using two types of laser cooling: one cooling the atoms moving in a specific direction and the other a standing wave in the opposite direction. Our model shows that the lasers' interplay within this environment is influenced by the characteristics of the lasers and the natural radiation from the atoms. As a result, the lasers' movements are interdependent in a non-linear way, which is also seen in the long-term movements of the atoms. The movements of the atoms over extended periods can be described in terms of the gradients of the lasers' frequencies. The unique feature of this model is that the atoms' movement distribution does not follow standard exponential patterns but rather shows sudden, large variations. The movements of the atoms can be better understood through the concept of the first passage time, which measures the time it takes for the atoms to move a certain distance. The statistical behavior of the atoms can be better described through the fractional Fokker-Planck equation, a non-standard approach that takes into account the complex interactions within the environment.

The cryptocurrency market is a rapidly evolving investment sector with significant interest from a diverse range of market participants due to its 24/7 trading availability and low entry barriers. The lack of24/7 human supervision has led to a dynamic market influenced by global events and news, with a significant majority of transactions executed by automated systems. Our study aims to investigate the cryptocurrency market by first identifying the leading currencies based on trading volume and then constructing a co-movement network from their price data. We utilize a graphical modeling approach to uncover both pairwise and high-order statistical dependencies within the market. The results indicate a weak market structure with a low number of interconnected cryptocurrencies at a pairwise level, but a more complex interdependence when considering high-order relationships.

This research employs high-level quantum chemical calculations to examine the impact of zero-point motion on the structure and stability of up to five-water and three-sulphuric acid-sized cluster ions. Our findings demonstrate a notable influence of zero-point motion on the stability of these cluster ions, with stability enhancements of 0.5 to 2.0 kJ/mol. Additionally, we observe a tendency for vibrational mode local mode character to promote stability through zero-point energy shifts. These insights are crucial in understanding the stability of larger binary sulphuric acid-water droplets, which play a crucial role in atmospheric new particle formation.

We establish a compactification of a broad class of metric spaces, including spaces derived from neural networks and group orbit spaces, by incorporating boundary elements. This enables us to compactify spaces of functions equivalent under a group action, thereby providing insights into the asymptotic behavior of functions under specific transformations, potentially offering a framework for understanding concepts such as scale invariance in machine learning.

The way solids respond to temperature gradients can be studied through the concept of thermal conductivity, 
which can be as intricate as electrical conductivity in the context of quantum Hall systems. 
In this study, a specific model is used to derive the vector potential that drives the flow of heat 
and how it is influenced by two temperature differences. 
Interestingly, when one temperature difference is held constant, 
the response to the other can be misinterpreted as an gravitational force in certain theories. 
However, within this research, this gravitational analogy fails in two key aspects: 
firstly, this gravitational effect does not necessarily cause the system to move in a specific direction, 
unlike what is suggested by the equivalence principle; 
secondly, conservation of energy dictates that this effect must be balanced by a related force 
acting in the opposite direction. 
These findings are further supported by experiments that have shown that 
systems with different properties respond differently to the simulated gravitational force.

The simplicity of learned functions is essential for generalizing well, and early interventions like holding model capacity or training data fixed aim to gauge its intrinsic properties. However, introducing training metrics such as weight magnitude or prediction uncertainty has a more substantial impact on generalization, effectively constraining the model to simpler solutions. Our research explores the geometric complexity of model decision boundaries in one-class classification problems and reveals a key finding: different model configurations produce distinct and quantifiable intrinsic complexities. Building on this insight, we've developed a novel measure of geometric complexity and used it to establish a new model of overfitting, which can predict model performance with high accuracy. Furthermore, this model demonstrates that even minor changes in network architecture can significantly influence geometric complexity and generalization, underscoring the need for careful consideration of intrinsic properties in promoting model simplification.

A new approach for analyzing the data from $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays is developed to directly extract the model-independent Wilson coefficients. The proposed method involves simultaneously fitting angular distribution data and control data from $B^0\to \mu^+\mu^-$ decays to determine the coefficients. The advantages of this method include eliminating background uncertainty and removing theoretical form factor uncertainties from the $B$ transition. The analysis also yields a direct measurement of background terms, providing a novel perspective on the data. The method has been successfully tested using simulated data from the LHCb experiment and demonstrates high potential for applying to real data once sufficient data is collected.

Automated essay scoring using automated grading systems has been around for decades, 
employing various machine learning and deep learning algorithms. Despite this, 
researchers have found that available datasets for training are often too small and 
limited in diversity, resulting in models that don't generalize well to unseen data. 
To address this issue, a common technique is data augmentation, which involves artificially 
expanding the size of a dataset by creating modified versions of existing samples. This study 
investigates the effectiveness of a new form of sentence-level data augmentation that leverages 
language models to create related sentences, and demonstrates its benefits when combined with 
a pre-trained transformer model for producing accurate automated essay scores.

Given a simplicial complex defining a tensor's marginalizations, we restrict them to rank one and analyze the resulting linear systems'marginal independence models'. We demonstrate existence and uniqueness of solutions under certain 'torical' conditions for a broad class of marginalizations, including a specific type defined by a closed subgraph's vertex deletions in a Markov graph. We develop efficient algorithms for these specific marginalizations and derive corresponding free energy maximization properties.

This study examines a dynamic model of social mobility across generations, 
where decisions about distributing opportunities impact future mobility patterns. 
We demonstrate the existence of multiple equilibria in this context and investigate 
the consequences of intergenerational transfers of opportunities as a means to correct market 
failures or implement social policy measures aiming to enhance mobility.

The symmetry of wave functions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wave function exchange statistics when the particles have opposite spatial momenta. This connection between parity and statistics appears to be fundamental, although the specific properties of the superexchange operator for particles with spin greater than 0 complicate its implementation in quantum mechanics.

We propose an upgrade to a signature scheme, allowing one signer to delegate another signer's ability to make valid, tamper-proof additions to a sequence of signed messages without exposing them. This upgrade is incorporated into a cryptocurrency framework, where the delegate can issue coins at specific addresses without disclosing their identity. This modification maintains the original properties of security and privacy while improving transaction efficiency and size by limiting the use of cryptography to just the receiving end of a transaction.

We've developed a deterministic solver for systems of linear equations, Ach + b = 0, where A is an n x n matrix with entries in a specific algebraic structure and rank r. Our solver runs in O~(nr^(1+epsilon)) time, where epsilon can be arbitrarily small, improving upon the previously best O~(nr^(1.5)) solution by Woodruff and Thomas (2019) and the O~(nr^(1+sqrt{log n / log r}) ) time by Woodruff, Li, and Chan (2019). This result nearly matches lower bounds established by Li and Woodruff (2020) for a specific case where r is a power of n.

Researchers have made the first detection of events in proton-proton collisions at a high energy of 13 TeV, which result in the creation of three massive gauge bosons (topological classification W topological classification W topological classification Z, topological classification W topological classification W, topological classification Z, topological classification W topological classification Z, topological classification W, topological classification W topological classification W) that are extremely rare. Using the CMS experiment at the LHC, a total of 138 femtobarns of data was collected in 2016. This data was analyzed for a variety of final state signatures, which allowed scientists to compare observed results with predictions made using the Standard Model. Notably, the detection of events in the final state signature W topological classification W topological classification Z, which are expected to occur 0.04 times per femtobarn, was the first time this specific process has been observed. Furthermore, the measured cross section for this event was found to be in agreement with theoretical predictions, within one standard deviation.

Hebrew possesses unique writing characteristics, including a writing system lacking punctuation and word segmentation, which hinders Natural Language Processing tasks. Previous attempts to overcome these obstacles involved leveraging manually annotated data. This study presents an expanded, manually annotated Hebrew corpus with 10,939 sentences and 281,000 words. The corpus is used to test various Hebrew parsing approaches, including those based on neural networks. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the effectiveness of a new neural model in achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple annotation metrics.

We establish a new result regarding incompressible subsets of Euclidean space, demonstrating that for any finite set $X$ within the Euclidean space and any incompressible subset $S$ of $X$, there exists a function that maps $S$ into a lower-dimensional Euclidean space while preserving distances within a factor of $(1+\varepsilon)$, where the required dimensionality is determined by Euclidean geometry principles and logarithmic factors related to the size of $S$.

Recent advances in artificial intelligence have led to a surge in data-centric models, but their non-transparent decision-making processes and limited ability to generalize in data-sparse environments pose significant challenges. To address these issues, we introduce a novel framework for collaborative AI development that leverages human expertise through the Cooperative Data-Centric Foundation Model (CDFM) method. This model enables collaborative improvement of representations through cooperative foundations, ensuring human alignment and encouraging the creation of more trustworthy and effective representations. To validate our approach, we conduct experiments on two representation evaluation tasks, achieving superior results compared to current state-of-the-art models on image captioning and linearized visual task performance.

Current research has a significant knowledge gap in creating robust low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes that can handle channel distortions and memory, particularly in scenarios involving binary erasures without feedback. This paper presents a novel method for constructing LDPC codes that have strong performance capabilities in minimizing block error rates under such conditions. The proposed LDPC codes have a structured generator matrix and degree-degree correlation, which enhances their error correction capabilities. The research derives a truncated density evolution equation to analyze their performance in binary erasures, and uses this finding to develop a novel LDPC code construction algorithm using a graph-based approach. The proposed construction method has a polynomial time complexity and outperforms randomly constructed LDPC codes significantly in terms of performance efficiency.

To enhance the security of control systems against disturbances and inaccuracies, a method using Model Predictive Control (MPC) is employed, where a real-time feedback controller modifies an optimally planned trajectory. A newer framework, System Level Synthesis (SLS)-MPC, takes a different approach by considering the closed-loop system response as a combination of nominal disturbances and state changes, which allows for more comprehensive safety guarantees in complex environments with intricate constraints. This paper demonstrates that SLS-MPC can be formulated as a Quadratic Program (QP) that finds the optimal nominal trajectory, trajectory modifications, and the optimal feedback gain simultaneously. Additionally, SLS-MPC is shown to maintain computational efficiency comparable to traditional MPC methods.

A critical flaw in the current implementation of quantum key distribution (QCD) keys has been exploited in a new study, where hackers can secretly monitor the conversation and recover the key. A real-world test demonstrated that even basic hacking techniques involving standard, easily obtainable equipment can trigger the QCD's error detection mechanisms while the hackers successfully establish the key. The study's findings emphasize the necessity of developing more resilient QCD systems capable of withstanding the QCD's limitations in real-world applications.

Recent studies have demonstrated the capability of large-scale language models to be taught a range of tasks without additional training, simply by observing examples provided in text. This phenomenon has been observed across various models, leading researchers to investigate the underlying mechanisms. This research aims to examine how large-scale models utilize prelearned knowledge to tackle in-context tasks. We conduct a comprehensive analysis of two aspects: the influence of model size and the quality of pretraining data. We employ two metrics to measure these effects, including mutual information and the confidence confidence correlation, using a diverse set of benchmarks. We also perform ablation studies to isolate the contributions of different knowledge types. We discovered that large models primarily rely on two types of learned knowledge: syntactic and semantic. We also found that when multiple models are presented with various input examples, they tend to display consistent internal states correlated with task outputs. This behavior persists even when the model size or pretraining data quality changes. This research offers novel insights into the capabilities and limitations of large models and their use of prelearned knowledge.

We investigated how the central regions of galaxy clusters evolve over time through numerical simulations, incorporating various initial conditions and physical processes. Our results show that in low-entropy clusters, the central regions collapse in a "shattering" pattern, whereas in field-free clusters with stronger entropy, a "growth" pattern emerges. These findings align with previous theoretical and observational studies. When simulating the field-free case, we observed an increase in the number of blue stellar objects, consistent with previous research. However, when simulating a case with a field-free environment, we found that the number of blue stellar objects decreased. These differences can be attributed to the central collapse of low-entropy clusters in the field-free scenario. In contrast, when simulating a case with a field-free environment, we found that the primary mechanism for shock heating prevents significant cooling in these regions. These findings suggest that a field-free environment is necessary for the development of blue stellar objects in these regions.

The Abstract for T. Mannel's (Uni. of Regensburg, Germany) presentation at the 2011 European Conference on Nuclear Physics in Jerusalem, Jordan, summarizes a review of experimental progress in $C\!P$ violation research in beauty- and charm-hadron decays, noting that recent findings have provided compelling evidence for subleading $C\!P$-violating effects, while whether these findings reflect the predicted leading standard-model predictions remains an open question.

New high-energy string interactions have been discovered in 10D open superstring theory. These amplitudes have a unique structure, significantly different from previously known hard string results. Their discovery brings the total number of known high-energy string interactions in 10D superstring theory to six. Notably, a relationship has been found between these new amplitudes and their fermionic counterparts. Specifically, it has been proven that interaction amplitudes involving one negative-helicity photon and the rest positive-helicity are directly related. This brings the total number of known high-energy string interactions in 10D superstring theory to seven. This brings the total number of known high-energy string interactions in 10D superstring theory to seven. This brings the total number of known high-energy string interactions in 10D superstring theory to seven.

To effectively manage the growing number of mobile devices and data traffic, future wireless networks will need advanced management systems that can adapt to changing requirements in real-time. This work presents novel methods for managing mobile data traffic and network costs through a specialized management system, which uses machine learning and predictive algorithms to optimize base station operations and enhance user experience. The approach involves using historical data to train algorithms that can predict and control network behavior, allowing for efficient use of network resources and reduced expenses. The methods are supported by a software platform that provides tools for data analysis, visualization, and automated decision-making. The results show that the system can significantly improve the quality of service and lower operational costs.

In the field of speech synthesis, there is a growing need to develop techniques for speech synthesis without requiring any pre-existing speech data due to concerns over privacy and intellectual property. To address this challenge, we propose a zero-resource speech synthesis approach using only letters as input. The method involves creating a dictionary of basic speech units from the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) chart and assigning them no additional sub-units of sound. These units are then combined in a specific order determined by the speech signal, resulting in a sequence of the basic speech units that are used to train a neural network for synthesizing speech. The results show that the speech synthesized with this approach is of sufficient quality to be useful, although further study is required.

Optimizing complex systems with multiple interacting components often involves non-convex constraints, making it challenging to achieve optimal solutions using traditional methods. To address this challenge, we propose a multi-stage optimization approach with tightly coupled tightness (MSCCCT) algorithm that leverages data-driven methods to generate adaptive constraints. These constraints ensure a high degree of accuracy in balancing the competing goals of computational efficiency and solution quality. Our approach uses localized linear approximations to model system behavior, which are then refined through iterative feedback from solving the optimization problems. By continuously adjusting the parameters based on the dual variables obtained from each stage of the solution process, we ensure that the algorithm converges to high-quality solutions in a computationally feasible amount of time. Our method has been successfully applied to a variety of challenging problems, including planning efficient movements for robotic systems in environments with obstacles, and designing optimal control strategies for vehicles to avoid collisions.

We establish precise limits on how quantum states can be converted from one form to another using probabilistic methods. Our approach involves developing a novel framework for comparing mixed quantum states that is both mathematically rigorous and has practical applications in the study of quantum resources. Using this framework, we can derive a set of conditions that completely determine if one state can be transformed into another through a specific type of physical process. Our findings include specific limits on the success rates of these transformations, a concept known as the deterministic optimal success rate. This framework has various applications, such as setting boundaries on how much asymmetry a quantum state might have and investigating the quality of quantum random number generators.

We investigated the movement of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, both theoretically and through experimentation. Upon acceleration, the liquid's surface tilts due to the interplay between gravity and the horizontal inertial force. However, the motion isn't uniform; it oscillates as the carrier moves up and down, causing the coffee's surface area to expand and contract in a rhythmic pattern. This dynamic movement increases the coffee's kinetic energy beyond what initial conditions would suggest. To understand this phenomenon, we developed a model that compares the coffee to an inverted pendulum whose center of mass moves in sync with its support structure. By applying a mathematical framework, we demonstrated that the coffee's energy grows over time due to parametric resonance, which occurs when the frequency of vertical movements matches the coffee's natural swinging frequency. This discovery has the potential to be utilized in designing systems that convert mechanical energy into electrical energy through the coffee's motion.

In our research, we enhance the accuracy of a decentralized machine learning algorithm by having network nodes with data and connections. The data at each node follows a distinct probability distribution, and our goal is to develop a robust decentralized algorithm that's resilient to variations in distribution. Since non-convex machine learning problems are difficult to solve precisely, we introduce a new method that uses a modified version of a well-known optimization technique to find a near-best solution within a certain error margin. Our method builds on prior decentralized algorithms and incorporates simple, connection-based updates that don't rely on the number of nodes in the network. Mathematical analysis confirms the effectiveness of this approach, and our experiments verify these findings in practice.

We investigate the utility of hydrodynamic attractors in modeling the initial stages of nuclear collisions. By employing a simplified scalar field model, atomic, nuclear, and quark-gluon plasma collisions exhibit distinct initial states characterized by varying degrees of equilibrium. Equations describing both field and fluid dynamics allow us to delve into the concept of hydrodynamic attractors and their utility in relativistic nuclear collisions. By leveraging numerical solutions, an empirical formula is established for the specific initial energy density in terms of transverse energy and rapidity width. Hydrodynamic attractors demonstrate effective production of entropy and particles, outperforming traditional Navier-Stokes equations in the early stages of such events.

Observations from the ALMA telescope have revealed the presence of high-velocity protostellar jets in multiple molecular star-forming regions. These ALMA observations have revealed that the gas surrounding a jet source is being heated and thus appears to be emitting more light. This indicates that the jet is interacting with the surrounding gas and thus contributing to the mass and energy balance in the star-forming region. This in turn supports the theory that the jet is part of a larger outflow system rather than a separate phenomenon. This study aims to provide a systematic approach to identifying the signs of a jet in the gas-emitting material surrounding a jet source and to use these signs to track the spatial development of jet-sustained outflows over large distances.

This research focuses on developing a balanced control strategy that maintains a stable supply of nonlinear systems under constrained conditions. We begin by defining a novel measure known as the saturation level set, representing nonlinear expectations regarding system saturation states. Building upon this concept, we propose a novel invariance criterion for saturation sets and an innovative nonlinear system control method based on this criterion. This new approach utilizes a saturated expectation as its core principle, enabling balanced control between performance and saturation for constrained nonlinear systems. Moreover, we demonstrate through a simulation that this proposed method effectively achieves balanced control in constrained nonlinear systems.

This research project focuses on identifying and estimating the Keplerian elements of Jupiter-orbiting satellites affected by solar radiation pressure semi-secular resonances. Utilizing established analytical theories of planetary motion, we have developed a method to pinpoint these resonances for each satellite and created a corresponding plotting tool. By applying this methodology to actual observational data of 13 Jupiter moons obtained from the NASA Horizons database, we have both theoretically and computationally determined their dates of first Solar Radiation Pressure resonance encounters. Furthermore, this study aims to provide precise predictions for future resonances and offers potential applications for monitoring missions like the Juno spacecraft.

We examine the differences between two methods of modeling the interaction of light with materials based on the principles of first-order physics: the velocity gauge and the Coulomb gauge. In the Coulomb gauge approach, the vector potential is smoothed out using a smooth window function to prevent numerical issues. A key finding is that introducing this smoothing has significant implications for the model's Hermiticity and its invariance under gauge transformations. The model's consistency under gauge transformations relies heavily on enforcing strict momentum conservation, a requirement that is not always feasible in practical applications. The limitations of our approach are particularly evident when trying to model real-space phenomena like charge transfer within a real-space tight-binding framework.

This study focuses on solving object-centric perception tasks for category-level objects in both 2D and 3D keypoints, considering that specific object identities are not known a priori. This approach is relevant in various real-world applications like urban planning and search and rescue operations. To tackle these challenges, we develop novel, robust models for 2D and 3D keypoints that are resilient to diverse domain shifts and noise. Our models draw on optimal transport theory, resulting in a flexible framework adaptable to various settings. We validate our approach through comprehensive simulations and real-world experiments across multiple datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in achieving accurate pose estimation, shape reconstruction, and providing analytical insights into our methods.

We discuss a graphic representation, a confidence disc and square, that visually depicts two-dimensional confidence regions for a parameter pair consisting of a location parameter and a precision parameter in a de Finetti distribution.

A new statistical method is developed for basket trials to assess the effectiveness of a new treatment across multiple patient groups, using data from similar past trials, to "borrow" information and increase statistical power while reducing sample size. The proposed approach employs hierarchical Bayesian models to calculate the necessary sample size, using clinical significance as a key factor. We examine two types of statistical tests - frequentist and likelihood-ratio - in contrast to our method. We demonstrate the utility of the new approach through simulation studies and a real-world trial analysis of an anti-cancer drug tested on three distinct types of cancer.

To improve motion control systems' efficiency and robustness, a new modification to the sequential loop closing strategy is developed for systems with linear parameter varying characteristics. The proposed modification enhances SLC performance by incorporating a filter that takes into account interaction dynamics between channels. A filter synthesis method based on a LMI formulation is also introduced to robustly minimize the effects of parameter variations and uncertainties. The result is a two-stage control design that simplifies high-precision system development by exploiting couplings rather than ignoring them. The effectiveness of this modification is demonstrated through experimental results on a nanometer-scale positioning table.

Deep learning has significantly impacted medical image analysis, particularly in the area of image registration. Nonetheless, traditional image registration techniques generally involve a computationally expensive full-to-full process. This can be both time-consuming and resource-intensive. In contrast, recent research has explored partial-to-partial registration, which focuses on aligning specific subsets of images. This approach has the potential to reduce the time and resources required. However, such research has so far been limited to a fully-supervised framework. This has led to the development of a novel fully-supervised method called the Registration Network with Embeddings and Features (PRNet), which outperforms existing state-of-the-art registration techniques in multiple metrics. While PRNet's performance is impressive, it does require access to complete images, which may not always be feasible in real-world scenarios. To address this limitation, we propose an innovative self-supervised approach based on PRNet, which enables partial-to-partial registration without the need for complete images. To our knowledge, this is the first registration network to be adapted for self-supervised learning. Our experiments demonstrate that this new self-supervised method rivals the performance of existing state-of-the-art registration techniques across multiple metrics.

A countable group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. This paper demonstrates that certain quotients of the generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar group $G_n$ have the property $R_\infty$, which implies that specific quotients made from direct products of free abelian groups also exhibit property $R_\infty$.

To find out how and when the Standard Model vacuum will decay, we need to know the true value of the Higgs mass. The fact that it lies within an unstable range makes it crucial to obtain more precise measurements of its top quark's mass. We're analyzing a range of potential future collider options, ranging from improvements to LHC to compact muon colliders, to see which are most suitable for making the most accurate measurements. Our study shows that the best choices are either a 100 TeV proton collider or advanced muon colliders, both of which would provide the best top quark mass measurements.

A new technique is developed to determine the concentrations of precursors from time-resolved emission spectra using linear unmixing methods. This technique builds upon existing linearity-based approaches yet offers a significant advantage by providing a stable and accurate solution, even when faced with experimental inaccuracies. To achieve this, a modified objective function is optimized for the specific dynamics of unmixing coefficients in a trajectory basis framework. Under certain conditions, the method guarantees a unique solution that converges to the true values of the coefficients. The effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated through both simulated and real-world experiments involving the study of a photodynamic process and the mixing of two precursors with overlapping spectra.

We present the results of calculating the longitudinal and transverse distribution amplitudes for $D^*$ and $D^*_s$ mesons using a Bethe-Salpeter amplitude-based approach. Our calculations were carried out in two-momentum space with regulation via the principle of minimal distortion. The distribution amplitudes were also parameterized using a polynomial model. Notably, the $D^*$ and $D^*_s$ meson masses obtained through this method align with their experimental values. Furthermore, our results for the longitudinal and transverse distribution amplitudes of the $D^*$ meson and the longitudinal distribution amplitude of the $D^*_s$ meson agree with corresponding phenomenological and lattice gauge theory findings.

We derive novel characterizations of Gelfand-Shilov spaces using Fourier transforms. Specifically, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for a function to belong to these spaces. By S. Asai's theorem on hypercyclic operators, we demonstrate that certain modified Gaussian functions cannot be cyclic vectors for Toeplitz operators within any given subspaces of Schwartz space. This has implications for the spaces we are studying.

Segmenting objects in images is a highly desired task, but acquiring detailed annotations for multiple image modalities can be both costly and time-consuming. To address this issue, we focus on training an instance segmentation model for a target modality by leveraging existing annotations from a single Modality Cycle Consistent Prediction (MCPP)GAN, which is used to handle different image modalities. Our approach allows the model to learn meaningful features from other modalities without requiring detailed annotations for the target modality. By leveraging information from multiple modalities, our model achieves superior performance in handling various image types.

Our proposed method, Feature Mapping RNN, leverages a Radial Basis Function kernel to map video features to a space that better distinguishes future actions, allowing more precise predictions with reduced temporal distances. This approach excels in low frame-rate sequences and exhibits enhanced robustness to variations in mean body positions, achieving a notable improvement of 10% in mean absolute error compared to the CK40 dataset.

A comprehensive analysis of the ultraviolet continuum modeling of the April 12, 1985, UV flare from the pre-main sequence star AD Leo is presented in this study. By applying a two-zone model to the stellar atmosphere, the characteristics of the hot and cool zones are examined. The hot zone's temperature, density, and radial extent are found to be 30,000 K, 10^9 cm^-3, and 10^9 cm, respectively. The cool zone's temperature, density, and radial extent are found to be 8000 K, 10^10 cm^-3, and 10^9 cm. The application of this model to other T Tauri stars is also discussed.

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds using analytical methods. Our study begins by establishing a one-to-one correspondence between the space of gauge-invariant first-order deformations of these instants and the closed sections of the adjoint bundle. We then define the deformation complex and demonstrate its relationship to the cohomology groups of the nearly G2-manifold's twisted de Rham complex. As a result of this characterization, we successfully identify the structure tree for all 32 known nearly split G2-manifolds deformations.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is termed $C$-normal if it satisfies the equation $TC^*T=C^*TC^*$. The purpose of this paper is to investigate the $C$-normal weighted composition operator $W_\phi^{\psi, \sigma, C}$ on the space of holomorphic functions on the open unit disk of the complex plane. Under the condition that the operator is $C$-normal on $H^2$, the weight function $\phi$ is determined by a function of a specific form involving the operator's parameters.

This paper delves into a type of partition that excludes elements divisible by a prime number $p$. Specifically, we focus on $p$-core $p'$-partitions with a high degree, where the number is represented as $n$. These specialized partitions are known for their connection to various mathematical problems, including high values of the divisor function and the coefficient of circular partitions. We establish a new finding that the number of such partitions with a value of $n$ grows at a rate of $n^{2/3}$ times an exponential factor, specifically $e^{2/3\beta_2(p)(\ln n)^{2/3]}$, where $\beta_2(p)$ is a constant unique to each prime number $p$. Additionally, we present a detailed algorithm to calculate the set $\mathcal{A}_k(p)$ for any given prime number $p$ and non-negative integer $k$.

Neural Occupancy Networks (NONN) are advanced methods that utilize 3D voxel grids to represent complex scenes, effectively detecting and segmenting three-dimensional objects. However, NONNs face significant challenges due to real-world variations in object appearance, orientation, and scale. Although multiple techniques have been developed to address these issues, they often fail to provide satisfactory solutions. In response, we introduce a novel technique called Topic-Specific Poissonian Sphere Growth, which tackles these challenges by incorporating multiple, distinct representations of a scene. Our approach excels in handling real-world variations by generating diverse configurations of a scene, thereby enhancing the model's performance. In experimental evaluations, we demonstrate that TPC outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both robustness and accuracy.

We examine media access methods in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks, which are sensitive to interference due to their frequency-modulated nature. A novel approach is proposed, incorporating a medium access control (MAC) layer to mitigate inter-radar interference and enhance the performance of multiple FMCW radars operating in close proximity. This method combines Fine Timing Measurement (FTM) messages from IEEE 802.11's Wireless LAN (WLAN) standard with Carrier Sense Multiple Access (CSMA) and Slotted ALOHA protocols. Our research also compares the performance of this MAC layer with and without Medium Sensing (MS), as well as evaluates the impact of network parameters on its efficacy.

Recent experiments employing a non-linear medium have been used to manipulate the entanglement of photons. Specifically, an active medium can introduce significant changes. However, an innovative approach employs a passive medium near resonance with one of the photons to induce superior changes. Researchers have now taken a theoretical stance, modeling a Hong-Ou-Mandel interference experiment incorporating a three-level lambda system in a interferometer. By applying a classical light source and adjusting experimental parameters such as detuning and input intensity, modifications in interference patterns can be induced. These changes offer a deeper understanding of the phenomenon and pave the way for further exploration into entangled photon interactions.

We calculate the elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces for torsion elements in the elliptic cohomology of a complex vector space, 
equipped with complex conjugation symmetry. Our approach utilizes the elliptical Cartan model to establish a elliptic isomorphism between CP spaces and the mapping spaces from the 2-sphere to an elliptic cohomology theory theory, 
which then facilitates a elliptic version of the Mahowald isomorphism.

Temporal Knowledge Graph Completion (KGC) involves predicting missing knowledge within a time-sensitive graph.
While KGC has seen significant advancements, most approaches overlook the representation of time, leading to limited performance when temporal knowledge is involved.
To overcome this shortcoming, our proposed method, Time-Learned Entity Representation (TiLER), incorporates a time dimension for each entity by assigning a vector to every (entity, timestamp) pair.
These vector representations enable the capture of entity behaviors over time and enhance knowledge completion capabilities.
To efficiently handle the increased complexity, TiLER employs a low-rank tensor model that can aggregate temporal knowledge and reduce model parameters without relying on a pre-set format for entity representations.
Extensive experiments conducted on three real-world datasets have demonstrated the superiority of TiLER over state-of-the-art methods, particularly in scenarios involving temporal knowledge completion.

The presence of sound from the ground has a significant influence on the propagation of electric charges in the atmosphere surrounding high voltage transmission lines experiencing backflashovers, thereby altering ionization patterns and ion mobility within the air. This effect is particularly pronounced in scenarios involving ground charges, which can be influenced by the soil's physical and chemical properties.

A concept known as Bell nonlocality without inequalities has been demonstrated through the use of a novel strategy that does not rely on precise correlations between shared measurements. This novel approach has enabled researchers to verify nonlocality even in the presence of noisy correlations. As a result, a perfect demonstration of Bell nonlocality without inequalities was achieved for the first time using non-primitive binary observables in a two-party system. This breakthrough shows that a perfect demonstration is possible as long as there is some level of nonlocal correlation greater than local correlation. This achievement was made possible through a suitable choice of non-primitive four-level systems and a non-primitive binary observable with a value range of two.

In flat band systems under the influence of an electric field, all states are degenerate and therefore a slight disturbance causes the states to localize. Our research focuses on whether a flat band can remain non-localized in a flat-band Mott insulator. We demonstrate that introducing a next-nearest neighbor hopping in the Hubbard model on a 2D Kagome lattice doesn't destroy the non-zeromagnetic ground state under open boundary conditions, but does under periodic ones. Furthermore, our study reveals a unique magnetic phase diagram under open boundary conditions that includes an unusual ferromagnetic state adjacent to the anti-ferromagnetic state, with an extended metallic region in between showing a charge density wave pattern.

A newly synthesized material, LdB$_{40}$, was found to be superconducting at approximately 9K based on experimental evidence. Recent theoretical research has suggested that LdB$_{40}$ could potentially be improved to become a high-temperature superconductor at higher pressures. However, our density functional theory and linear response calculations do not support the presence of a significant superconducting gap in LdB$_{40}$, which could be attributed to the presence of dangling bonds in the material. As an alternative, we propose a similar material HBL$_{39}$S as a high-temperature superconductor with a critical temperature above 20K.

The frequency distribution of run lengths in flattened partitions of a positive integer $n$ is analyzed. The findings demonstrate that this frequency distribution tends towards a Gaussian pattern as $n$ increases. The confirmation of this frequency distribution is verified through three different methodologies – numerical evidence, an examination of the underlying combinatorial structure, and an exploration of a corresponding statistical model. The corresponding statistical model is shown to accurately reflect the physical phenomenon of long-range one-dimensional heat conduction in a finite, homogeneously lattice-structured system with constant heat diffusion.

We categorize irreducibly stiff representations of a free group into distinct equivalence classes based on their image's equivalence, where two representations are considered equivalent if their images are virtually isomorphic. It is demonstrated that certain categories of arithmetic groups possess irreducibly stiff representations where virtually isomorphic images necessarily share the same integral closed geodesic growth rates. This finding is applied to the special linear groups $SL_2(\mathbb Z)$, $SL_3(\mathbb Z)$, and a range of other arithmetic groups parameterized by integers.

Automotive driving systems designed to operate in the event of failure are being increasingly utilized as advanced features in modern vehicles. A key example is the widely implemented Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS), such as lane departure warning systems and adaptive cruise control. This paper presents the formal design and comprehensive verification of a highly automated driving system operating on this principle. By employing probabilistic hybrid automata to model the system, which functions alongside continuous distance regulation, trajectory planning, and speed control, the authors derive and verify its safety properties through model checking, thereby also establishing liveness properties.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as neuroscience, finance, and network science is crucial for several reasons. These systems evolve over time and are continually impacted by external influences, making it essential to consider dynamic clustering that takes into account temporal changes. We employ a data-driven method to detect influences within time-series data, using it to define similarity between system nodes and develop an algorithm for classifying similar systems into distinct groups. This data-centric approach to clustering dynamic time-series data is demonstrated using two examples: a network of coupled oscillators and a set of time series stocks.

Recent research has highlighted Leibniz's use of a fundamental theorem linking differentiation and integration in a crucial aspect of his calculus development. This research modernized calculus by drawing on key concepts from Riemann integration theory, measure theory, and nonstandard analysis. Despite its significance, a crucial question remains unanswered: what specific problem drove Leibniz to discover and apply this theorem in a critical stage of his calculus evolution? This paper aims to address this gap by examining a related finding that connects differential and difference calculus.

We've developed a theoretical framework for predicting HI intensity mapping experiments using $n$-body simulations and cosmological perturbation theory, specifically tailored for high-redshift ranges. By simulating halos and matter distribution within different scenarios, we established a transfer function that links these distributions. Our model incorporates two effects - one-body signal and line distortion - and assessed the impact of cutting off large-scale foreground noise on power spectrum estimation. Our analysis reveals that foreground removal significantly influences our understanding of foreground noise and power spectra, with our model showing reasonable agreement with existing simulations. Our model demonstrates a substantial computational advantage over full simulations, enabling faster and more efficient predictions that can guide future intensity mapping projects.

This review collects and discusses key results from contemporary research connecting operators on a separable, complex Hilbert space with a specific set of cardinal values, particularly focusing on operator independence dimensions and their relationship to other operator cardinal invariants such as spectrum ranks and partial isometry ranks. Relevant operators include non-zero compact, nilpotent, Drazin invertible, and Drazin normal operators. The underlying concept relies on a generalized matrix representation method that can express certain classes of operators in terms of block matrices with specific constraints on their diagonal components.

One of the key areas influencing system context within a smart home is the advanced technology that supports it. Despite significant advancements, there is still room for improvement in developing context-aware systems. Developing such systems requires understanding and utilizing the environment's setting and the individual user's behavior. To address this challenge, we have designed a document-based hybrid recommender system that provides personalized recommendations based on a user's past behavior and current document setting. Our approach combines deep learning techniques with a unique feature of leveraging the environment's context. Our proposed system has been tested and validated through thorough experimentation, demonstrating its effectiveness in providing accurate and relevant recommendations in a real-world setting.

We develop a new trace function for matrices that meets the requirements for verifying the independence of random matrices using the criteria established by Voiculescu. This method involves augmenting matrices with the identity matrix and applying a specific transformation, which also has significant implications for understanding the spectral properties of matrices. Furthermore, we explore a relationship between our method and the concept of "conditional freeness" and demonstrate its applicability to cases involving non-commutative polynomials and quaternions.

This paper re-examines the monitoring of properties over time for both discrete and continuous systems, using techniques from supervised learning to create tight approximations for future property satisfaction. It specifically addresses the limitations of using traditional metrics by proposing a more nuanced approach that generates data-dependent guarantees. The research focuses on monitoring timed properties and provides solutions for handling multiple, potentially unbounded variables in diverse system contexts.

The decay $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi \pi^0 \eta$ is examined in detail to understand molecular contributions near thresholds. An in-depth investigation of this decay is conducted using an innovative approach that incorporates both initial and final state interactions within the $\bar B_s^0$ via the effective Hamiltonian. By employing an innovative method to handle intermediate meson resonances in a manner that adheres to unitarity and analyticity, we identify that the $a_0(980)$ contributes significantly to this decay, with potential detection at LHCb experiments.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera utilizes four individually controlled beams to expand the observational capabilities of the Very Large Telescope Interferometer by incorporating a rapid acquisition system. These cameras have been installed at all four E-UTLUs and have been thoroughly characterized using both on-sky observations and laboratory settings. The on-sky data revealed that the camera's optical system maintains stability over time, with the centroid position variation staying under 0.05 degrees, and the relative intensity balance between beams remains consistent with variations of less than 0.1%. The radiation source's point spread function exhibits stable structure across the field of view, with the differential aberrations affecting the field less than 0.02 degrees. The results demonstrate that the GRAVITY acquisition camera functions as intended, with the observed performance aligning with the predictions made during the camera's development stage.

We examine the impact of dimension-dependent parameters on the approximate solution size of the Generalized k-Center problem, where clients have distinct weights and a metric space is defined by a metric. The Generalized k-Center problem involves selecting k centers from a set of n points to minimize the maximum distance between any point and its nearest center, where the distance is weighted by the point's associated weight.

Our research focuses primarily on the 2-Approximation algorithm for Generalized k-Center on a set of points in a space with a finite doubling dimension. A 2-Approximation algorithm is presented, yielding a solution size within a factor of O(k log^2(k)) of the optimal value. This approximation is tight up to logarithmic factors, demonstrating that achieving an approximation better than O(k^(1+ε)) would contradict a long-standing hypothesis in theoretical computer science.

We also investigate the performance of a similar approximation on a set of points with a small doubling dimension d, proving an approximation of O(k^(1+ε)(log k)^(2d/3)) by reducing Generalized k-Center to the standard k-Center problem. This result shows the first instance where a parameter-dependent approximation better than a factor of k is achievable with a small number of parameters.
